phase1.intro:
This is opening day — the smallest possible version of the whole JavaFX pipeline, actually wired up and running.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: What order do I actually build things in?
dialogue: Inside start(), you build the window from the inside out: create your content first (a Label), then a layout container ([[term:StackPane]], which stacks children on top of each other and centers them by default), then wrap that in a Scene with a pixel width and height.

stickyNote.definition: A JavaFX window is built inside-out: create the content nodes, put them in a layout container (like StackPane), then wrap that in a Scene.

topics.buttonText: What are the three calls that actually open the window?
dialogue: `primaryStage.setTitle()` puts text in the title bar, `primaryStage.setScene(scene)` hangs your display in the window, and `primaryStage.show()` is the one that actually makes it visible — [[warn:forget show() and you'll have built a perfectly valid Scene that nobody ever sees]].

stickyNote.flavor: 👁️ show() is what actually makes it visible
stickyNote.definition: setTitle() labels the window, setScene() attaches the Scene, and show() is the call that finally displays it — forgetting show() leaves nothing visible.

topics.buttonText: What changes if I use a VBox instead of a StackPane?
dialogue: The second class, SecondJavaFXWindow, swaps StackPane for a [[term:VBox]] — same three-piece pipeline (nodes → layout → Scene), just a different shelf shape. That's the pattern for the rest of the unit: the pipeline never changes, only the layout and nodes do.

stickyNote.definition: The nodes → layout → Scene pipeline stays the same regardless of which layout container (StackPane, VBox, etc.) you choose.

phase1.openingDialogue: Every JavaFX app follows the same pipeline — nodes, then a layout container, then a Scene — and show() is what finally makes it visible. 🧱

phase2.errorMessage:
Test.java:9: error: cannot find symbol
    public void start(Stage primaryStage) {
                     ^
  symbol:   class Stage
  location: class Test
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:cannot find symbol: class Stage]] — the compiler has no idea what Stage means, because the file never imports it.

start(Stage primaryStage) uses the Stage type in its method signature, so [[key:the compiler needs to see import javafx.stage.Stage before it reads that line]] — without it, Stage is just an unrecognized word as far as javac is concerned, same as if you'd typed a made-up class name. JavaFX splits its classes across several packages (javafx.application, javafx.stage, javafx.scene, and more), so it's easy to import Scene and Label and forget the one that's arguably the most central class in the whole app.

phase3.openingDialogue: Let's create your first JavaFX window! 🪟

mcq.question:
You write a full, correct start() method — but you forget to call launch(args) in main(), and call start() directly instead: new Test().start(new Stage()). What happens?

A) The window opens normally — start() is all that matters
B) A runtime exception, because the JavaFX Application Thread and toolkit were never initialized by launch()
C) The compiler rejects the program
D) The window opens but is permanently blank

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a JavaFX program that:
1. Creates a Stage with title "My JavaFX App"
2. Creates a Label with text "Welcome to JavaFX!"
3. Uses a StackPane as the root layout
4. Creates a Scene with size 500x400
5. Shows the window

Inherit from Application and use launch() in main.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:the JavaFX toolkit only initializes once per JVM]] — that's part of why launch() insists on doing the setup instead of letting you construct a Stage with new anywhere in your code. Try to call launch() a second time in the same running app and it throws — one storefront, one grand opening.
